title: Enums, value conversions and owned types
summary: Store enums as text, map your own types with converters, and keep small value objects inside their owner's table.

steps.title: Enums
body: An enum property maps to an integer column by default:
public Genre Genre { get; set; }      // "Genre" INTEGER NOT NULL: 0, 1, 2
Integers are compact, but a row holding `1` means nothing to someone reading the table, and **reordering the enum silently changes the meaning of every stored row**. Storing the name is often safer:
Queries still work in C# terms: `db.Books.Where(b => b.Genre == Genre.Science)` becomes `WHERE "b"."Genre" = 'Science'`.

code: public Shelf Shelf { get; set; } = Shelf.Bottom;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: The program reads the raw row with plain ADO.NET, under EF Core. `Genre` has a string conversion, so the column holds its name. `Shelf` has none, so it holds the number: `Bottom` is the third value, `2`.

steps.title: Value conversions
body: `HasConversion` works for any type: give it two expressions, *to the database* and *back*.
tags => string.Join(',', tags),                                       // to the column
The column is a single `TEXT` holding `"space,classic"`. Good uses: a strongly typed id (`record struct BookId(int Value)`), a unit (`Distance` stored in metres), a flag set.

The catch: the database only sees the converted value. `Where(b => b.Tags.Contains("space"))` cannot be translated, because SQL does not know your comma format. Convert values you **store and compare whole**, not values you need to search inside.

steps.prompt: Store a `TimeSpan` as a number of whole minutes.
steps.explain: `HasConversion` takes the two directions. `TotalMinutes` is the whole length in minutes (`Minutes` is only the minutes *part*, 0 to 59), and `TimeSpan.FromMinutes` turns the number back.

steps.title: Owned types
body: Some classes have no identity of their own. An `Address` belongs to a customer; it is not a row anyone looks up by id. Mark it **owned**, and its properties become columns of the owner's table:
public Address Home { get; set; } = new();

The `Customers` table gets `Home_Street` and `Home_City`. Loading a customer always loads its address; there is no `DbSet<Address>`. Owned types are how EF Core models **value objects** from domain-driven design.
The Fluent API spelling is `model.Entity<Customer>().OwnsOne(c => c.Home);`.

code: public Address Home { get; set; } = new();
public Address Work { get; set; } = new();
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=shop.db");
steps.explain: Each owned property gets its own set of columns, prefixed with the property name. No table is created for `Address` itself.

steps.prompt: Owned type, or an entity of its own?
items: A GPS position: latitude and longitude
An author, shared by many books
A library branch that members visit
A product category you can rename for all products
steps.explain: A value with no identity, owned by exactly one thing, is an owned type. Something shared, looked up, or changed in one place for many owners needs its own table and key.

steps.title: A film catalogue
prompt: Write a `Film` entity and a `CinemaDb` context (`Data Source=films.db`, `DbSet<Film> Films`):
- `Rating Rating`, where `enum Rating { U, PG, Twelve, Fifteen, Eighteen }` is stored **as text**
- `TimeSpan Length`, stored as an integer number of **minutes**
- `Money Price`, an **owned** type with `int Amount` (in cents) and `string Currency`
Configure it with the Fluent API in `OnModelCreating` (or `[Owned]` for `Money`, your choice). Declare the enum and `Money` too.
starter: enum Rating { U, PG, Twelve, Fifteen, Eighteen }
solution: enum Rating { U, PG, Twelve, Fifteen, Eighteen }
public Money Price { get; set; } = new();
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=films.db");
template: dojoDb.Films.Add(new Film { Title = "Alien", Rating = Rating.Fifteen, Length = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(117), Price = new Money { Amount = 450, Currency = "EUR" } });
dojoDb.Films.Add(new Film { Title = "Up", Rating = Rating.U, Length = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(96), Price = new Money { Amount = 300, Currency = "EUR" } });
object? Col(string name) { for (var i = 0; i < dojoRow.FieldCount; i++) if (dojoRow.GetName(i) == name) return dojoRow.GetValue(i); return null; }
Dojo.Eq("Rating is stored as text", "Fifteen", Col("Rating")?.ToString());
Dojo.Eq("Length is stored as minutes", "117", Col("Length")?.ToString());
Dojo.Eq("Price lives in the Films table (Price_Amount)", "450", Col("Price_Amount")?.ToString());
Dojo.Eq("reads back the enum and the length", "Up 01:36:00", dojoUp.Title + " " + dojoUp.Length);
Dojo.Eq("reads back the owned price", 300, dojoUp.Price.Amount);
hints: `[Owned]` on `Money` is all an owned type needs.
